intro.html: Three Latin roots do a great deal of work in English. vert (also spelled vers) means turn, as in reverse. ject means throw, as in reject. tract means pull or draw, as in tractor and attract. Put a prefix in front, and each root turns, throws or pulls in a new direction.

vert, vers = turn. ject = throw. tract = pull, draw. Find the root, then ask where the prefix sends it: a- away, ad- toward, sub- under, de- down, inter- between, con- together, pro- forward, in- not.

Each memory hook below acts out the parts. Say them out loud (de-JECT-ed: thrown down), look at the picture, then check the meaning against the sentences. The parts are a clue; the sentence has the last word.

words.def: to turn away; to keep something bad from happening
words.ex: Pip {averted} his eyes so he would not spoil the surprise in the gift bag.
words.ctx: The crew worked through the night to patch the leaking dam, and their effort {averted} a flood that would have swamped the whole valley.
words.etym: From Latin avertere, “to turn away”: ab (away) + vertere (to turn).

mn.text: Captain Sven sees the rock ahead and turns the wheel hard; by turning away in time, he {averts} a crash.

scene.alt: A ship's captain turns the wheel hard to steer away from a rock in the sea.

words.def: harmful or unfavorable; working against you
words.ex: The soccer final was put off a week because of {adverse} weather: hail, lightning and high winds.
words.ctx: Despite {adverse} conditions, including a broken-down bus and a cold, steady rain, the band reached the parade on time and played the whole route.
words.etym: From Latin adversus, “turned toward, facing, opposed,” from advertere: ad (toward) + vertere (to turn).
words.note: Adverse describes things and conditions (adverse weather, adverse effects). Don’t confuse it with averse, which describes a person’s dislike: averse to risk.

mn.cue: AD-VERSE: the wind TURNS against you
mn.text: Ivy runs east with her kite, but the wind turns and blows hard the other way; {adverse} winds work against her.

scene.alt: A girl struggles to hold her kite as a strong wind blows against her.

words.def: able to do many different things, or to be used in many ways
words.ex: A {versatile} player, Rosa can pitch, catch and cover first base.
words.ctx: Unlike his brother, who could make only pancakes, Omar was a {versatile} cook: soup, curry, bread and birthday cakes all came out of his kitchen with equal skill.
words.etym: From Latin versatilis, “able to turn; turning easily from one task to another,” from versare, “to keep turning.”

mn.cue: VERSE-atile: sings VERSES, plays it all
mn.text: Tia sings the verses, strums the guitar, beats the drum and plays the fiddle, turning easily from one to the next: she is {versatile}.

scene.alt: A smiling musician on a stage surrounded by a guitar, a drum, a violin and a microphone, ready to play them all.

words.def: done by accident, without meaning to
words.ex: One {inadvertent} tap on the screen sent Grandpa’s message to the whole family instead of just to Nana Lou.
words.ctx: The spill was {inadvertent}; Dev had been watching the ball game on the screen, not his glass, when his elbow tipped it over.
words.etym: From inadvertence, from Medieval Latin inadvertentia: in- (not) + Latin advertere, “to turn toward,” as in turning your mind toward something.
words.note: An inadvertent mistake is not on purpose. It often comes from attention being somewhere else.

mn.cue: eyes IN the AD: a bump not meant
mn.text: Sami’s eyes are on the ad on the sign, not on the path, so he bumps a fruit cart. The bump is {inadvertent}: he did not mean it.

scene.alt: A boy reading a sign as he walks bumps into a fruit cart by accident, and lemons tumble.

words.def: to secretly weaken or overturn something established
words.ex: The sneaky player tried to {subvert} the rules by changing the score sheet when no one was looking.
words.ctx: The spy did not fight the kingdom openly; instead he worked to {subvert} it from within, quietly turning the queen’s own advisers against her.
words.etym: From Latin subvertere, “to turn from beneath, to overturn”: sub (under) + vertere (to turn).

mn.text: Sneaky Rex crawls under the king’s banquet table and tips it over from beneath. To {subvert} is to overturn from underneath.

scene.alt: A sneaky man crawls under a king's table and tips it over while the king looks shocked.

words.def: a guess made without enough proof
words.ex: Whether the old map leads to anything at all is pure {conjecture}.
words.ctx: With no fossils of its skin to study, the scientists could offer only {conjecture} about the creature’s color; their best guess was a dull green.
words.etym: From Latin conjectura, from conicere, “to throw together”: com (together) + jacere (to throw).

mn.text: Ada throws three clues together, a tipped vase, a paw print and a feather, and makes a guess: the cat chased a bird! Her {conjecture} may be wrong.

scene.alt: A woman with a magnifying glass looks at a tipped vase and a feather and guesses that the cat did it.

words.def: sad and discouraged; low in spirits
words.ex: After missing the bus to the big game, Kai sat on the curb looking {dejected}.
words.ctx: The players had counted on a win, so they trudged off the muddy field {dejected}, heads down and hardly speaking.
words.etym: From Latin deicere, “to throw down”: de (down) + jacere (to throw).

mn.text: The wind throws Jonah’s new kite down into the mud, and his spirits fall with it: he sits slumped and {dejected}.

scene.alt: A teenage boy sits sadly on the ground beside his kite, which has crashed into a puddle.

words.def: to break in with a remark while someone else is talking
words.ex: Grandpa Gus likes to {interject} a joke in the middle of every story.
words.ctx: Professor Edwin was halfway through his long explanation when a student {interjected} a quick question, and he paused to answer it before going on.
words.etym: From Latin intericere, “to throw between”: inter (between) + jacere (to throw).

mn.text: Mom and Dad are talking about dinner when Pip throws one word in between them: “Pizza!” He {interjects}.

scene.alt: A boy jumps between his talking parents and shouts his own idea for dinner.

words.def: hard to manage, control or solve
words.ex: The {intractable} goat refused to leave the porch, no matter how hard we pulled.
words.ctx: Most leaks are quickly fixed, but the old barn roof proved {intractable}: every patch failed, and new drips appeared with each storm.
words.etym: From Latin intractabilis: in (not) + tractabilis (manageable), from tractare, “to handle,” from trahere, “to pull.”

mn.text: Jamal pulls and pulls on the rope, but the donkey won’t move an inch. He can’t pull it or manage it: the donkey is {intractable}.

scene.alt: A farmer pulls hard on a rope, but a stubborn donkey refuses to move.

words.def: lasting much longer than expected or usual
words.ex: After a {protracted} search, Nana Lou found her glasses on top of her head.
words.ctx: What was meant to be a quick ten-minute meeting became a {protracted} debate that ran past dinner and left everyone tired and hungry.
words.etym: From Latin protrahere, “to drag forward, to draw out, to prolong”: pro (forward) + trahere (to pull).

mn.text: Professor Edwin’s “short” talk gets pulled out longer and longer, until his audience nods off. It is a {protracted} talk.

scene.alt: An old professor keeps talking at a podium while two students yawn and doze under a clock.

after.cap: The literal meaning is a clue; the sentence decides.

after.html: Two easy slips. Adverse describes conditions and effects (adverse weather, adverse side effects); averse describes a person who dislikes something (averse to risk). And an inadvertent mistake is an accident, not a choice: it happens without meaning to, often because attention was elsewhere.

opts.s: The hikers turned back an hour early to {avert} a soaking from the storm clouds rolling in.
opts.why: Turning back early kept the soaking from happening: they averted it.

items.q: The new allergy medicine had no ______ effects; Dad felt fine all week. Which word fits?
items.why: Effects that harm you are adverse. Averse describes a person who dislikes something (averse to spinach), not an effect.

items.q: True or false: an inadvertent mistake is one made on purpose.
items.why: False. Inadvertent means accidental: done without meaning to.

items.q: Which word does NOT come from the Latin root vert (turn)?
items.why: Overt (open, not hidden) only looks like a vert word: it comes through French from Latin aperire, to open. Divert, revert and convert all turn.

items.q: Taken part by part, dejected literally means…
items.why: de- (down) + ject (throw): a dejected person feels thrown down.

items.q: Type the word built from inter- (between) + ject (throw) that means “to break in with a remark.”
items.why: To interject is to throw a remark in between someone else’s words.
